title: Florida House, District 57
what_it_does: Represents District 57 (Part of Pinellas) in the Florida House; votes on state laws and the state budget.
verified_ballot_note: Candidate list taken from the Florida Division of Elections, 2026 general election candidate list on 2026-09-18 (https://dos.elections.myflorida.com/candidates/CanList.asp); statuses Qualified/Unopposed only. Counties from the Legislature's district listings.

candidates.name: Adam Anderson
candidates.background: Businessman who represents North Pinellas County in the Florida House and is seeking re-election. His website highlights work on streamlining permitting, virtual education and health screening programs.

roster_sources.title: Florida Division of Elections, 2026 general election candidate list

immigration.summary: Voted yes on SB 2-C (2025), which created the State Board of Immigration Enforcement, required state help with federal detainers, barred driver licenses for unauthorized immigrants, and funded an Unauthorized Alien Transport Program.

sources.title: Florida House roll-call vote, SB 2-C (Immigration), passage 85-30

abortion.summary: Voted yes on SB 300 (2023), the law that limits most abortions after six weeks of pregnancy.

sources.title: Florida House roll-call vote, SB 300 (Heartbeat Protection Act, six-week abortion limit), passage 70-40

guns.summary: Voted yes on HB 543 (2023), which allows carrying a concealed firearm without a state license.

sources.title: Florida House roll-call vote, CS/HB 543 (concealed carry without a license), passage 76-32

education_choice.summary: Voted yes on HB 1 (2023), which removed income limits and enrollment caps so state scholarship funds can follow any K-12 student to private or home education. His website also says Florida should lead the nation in flexible schooling options and career pathways.

sources.title: Florida House roll-call vote, CS/CS/CS/CS/HB 1 (universal school-choice scholarships), passage 83-27
Adam Anderson for Florida House (campaign website)

housing.summary: Anderson did not return the Tampa Bay Times questionnaire; the paper quoted his campaign site, which says the Legislature acted to reduce delays in housing construction by streamlining permitting and inspections to lower the cost of homes and renovations.
housing.quote: On the affordability front, we took decisive action to reduce costly delays in housing builds that make homes and renovations more expensive by streamlining inconsistent permitting and inspections processes.

sources.title: 2026 Florida election candidates: Midterm voter guide (Tampa Bay Times)

energy.summary: Voted for CS/CS/HB 1645 (2024), the 2024 energy law that removed climate change as a priority of state energy policy, repealed several renewable-energy goals and grant programs, banned offshore wind turbines in state waters and eased regulation of natural-gas pipelines; a vote for it is coded as leaning against promoting renewable energy.

sources.title: CS/CS/HB 1645 (2024) bill page - The Florida Senate

lgbtq.summary: Voted for SB 254 (2023), the 2023 law barring gender-affirming medical treatment for minors and restricting it for adults.

sources.title: SB 254 (2023) bill page - The Florida Senate

elections.summary: Voted for SB 7050 (2023), the 2023 elections law that raised penalties and shortened deadlines for third-party voter-registration groups and changed vote-by-mail and voter-roll procedures.

sources.title: SB 7050 (2023) bill page - The Florida Senate

insurance.summary: Voted for SB 2-A (Dec. 2022), the December 2022 property-insurance law that ended one-way attorney fees and assignment of benefits and created a state reinsurance program, a market-based approach; a vote for it is coded as leaning against more direct state intervention.

sources.title: SB 2-A (Dec. 2022) bill page - The Florida Senate

record.item: Voted for CS/CS/HB 1645 (2024), the 2024 energy law that removed climate change as a priority of state energy policy, repealed several renewable-energy goals and grant programs, banned offshore wind turbines in state waters and eased regulation of natural-gas pipelines; a vote for it is coded as leaning against promoting renewable energy.

Voted for CS/SB 102 (2023), the 2023 Live Local Act that put $711 million into state housing programs, required local governments to allow multifamily housing in commercial areas when at least 40 percent of units are affordable, and created property-tax exemptions for affordable developments; a vote for it is coded as leaning toward more government action on housing.

Voted for SB 2-C (2025), the February 2025 special-session immigration law that created a State Board of Immigration Enforcement, made entering Florida as an unauthorized immigrant a state crime and required local cooperation with federal detention.
Voted for SB 300 (2023), the 2023 law limiting most abortions to six weeks of pregnancy.
Voted for HB 543 (2023), the 2023 law allowing adults to carry a concealed firearm without a permit.
Voted for HB 1 (2023), the 2023 law that made every Florida student eligible for a state-funded scholarship usable at private schools or for home education.
Voted for SB 254 (2023), the 2023 law barring gender-affirming medical treatment for minors and restricting it for adults.
Voted for SB 7050 (2023), the 2023 elections law that raised penalties and shortened deadlines for third-party voter-registration groups and changed vote-by-mail and voter-roll procedures.

Voted for SB 2-A (Dec. 2022), the December 2022 property-insurance law that ended one-way attorney fees and assignment of benefits and created a state reinsurance program, a market-based approach; a vote for it is coded as leaning against more direct state intervention.

candidates.name: Wendy Hoy
candidates.occupation: Former teacher, Head Start director and home health/hospice educator
candidates.background: Oldsmar resident with a University of Michigan education degree who has worked as a teacher, Head Start director, home health and hospice educator, guardian ad litem and library board member. She says she entered the race after learning the incumbent had run unopposed.

roster_sources.title: Florida Division of Elections, 2026 general election candidate list

property_tax.summary: In a Tampa Bay 28 questionnaire she cited property-tax exemptions that create revenue loss for community services such as libraries as a reason she is running.

sources.title: Meet the candidates: Questionnaire for Florida State District 57 (Tampa Bay 28)

insurance.summary: Her issues page calls for property insurance rate caps and restoring homeowners' ability to challenge unfair insurer practices.

housing.summary: She proposes state incentives for small landlords who verifiably lower or stabilize rent.
housing.quote: Create state incentives for small landlords for verifiably lowering or stabilizing rent.

healthcare.summary: She supports accepting Medicaid expansion dollars.
healthcare.quote: Accept Medicaid expansion dollars which will lead to hundreds of thousands of working Floridians receiving affordable health coverage.

abortion.summary: She says she would return reproductive freedom and keep medical decisions between individuals and their doctors.
abortion.quote: Return reproductive freedom, safeguard LGBTQ+ families, and ensure personal medical decisions remain between individuals and their doctors.

lgbtq.summary: She says she would safeguard LGBTQ+ families and oppose government overreach into private lives; she does not name specific laws.

guns.summary: She supports gun-safety legislation, including restoring local governments' authority to enact gun-safety ordinances.
guns.quote: Common-sense gun safety legislation, including restoring local authority to enact gun safety ordinances.

elections.summary: She wants to expand vote-by-mail access and accept student IDs as voter ID.

environment.summary: She wants stronger coastal resilience and flood mitigation and would keep wetland mitigation within the same watershed.
environment.quote: Strengthen coastal resilience and flood mitigation protections.

growth.summary: Hoy told the Times she would put a moratorium on data-center development until the impacts are understood and regulations are in place, and listed restoring local control over zoning and environmental decisions as a top priority.
growth.quote: The first thing Florida should do is put a moratorium on data center development until the impacts of data centers is clearly understood and regulations are enacted to ensure transparency, governmental oversight...

sources.title: 2026 Florida election candidates: Midterm voter guide (Tampa Bay Times)

education_choice.summary: She calls for investing in strong public schools and ending book bans; she does not directly address vouchers.
education_choice.quote: Invest in strong public schools that serve every child.

veterans.summary: She supports expanding veterans' health care access with more clinicians, longer clinic hours and satellite mental-health sites.

energy.summary: Hoy said she would cap utility-rate increases and offer solar incentives as part of lowering household costs.

sources.title: 2026 Florida election candidates: Midterm voter guide (Tampa Bay Times)

other_issues.title: Data centers
other_issues.summary: She supports a moratorium on new data centers, including pausing incentives and fast-track approvals.

other_issues.title: Central database for assistance programs
other_issues.summary: Hoy said she would spend a $1 million appropriation on a central Pinellas County database of housing, food, utility, health, transportation and repair assistance, tied to the 2-1-1 social services line.

sources.title: 2026 Florida election candidates: Midterm voter guide (Tampa Bay Times)
